question: Which statement best describes Regex literals vs the RegExp constructor?
options: A character class matches one character from a set. Square brackets define your own set, like [aeiou] for a vowel or [a-z] for a lowercase letter, and a leading caret negates it: [^0-9] is any non-digit. Shorthand classes cover common sets: \d (digit), \w (word character: letters, digits, underscore), \s (whitespace), and their uppercase negations \D, \W, \S. A bare dot . matches any character except a newline.

You can write a pattern as a literal between slashes, /pattern/flags, which is compiled once when the script loads — best when the pattern is fixed. The RegExp constructor, new RegExp('pattern', 'flags'), builds a regex from a string at runtime, which you need when the pattern is dynamic (built from a variable). With the constructor, remember each backslash must itself be escaped in the string.

Quantifiers say how many times the preceding item may repeat. * means zero or more, + means one or more, and ? means zero or one (optional). Curly braces give exact counts: {3} is exactly three, {2,4} is two to four, {2,} is two or more. By default quantifiers are greedy (match as much as possible); add a ? to make them lazy (match as little as possible), as in .*?.

Anchors match positions, not characters. ^ asserts the start of the string (or line in multiline mode), $ asserts the end. Using both, like /^\d+$/, forces the entire string to match the pattern rather than just containing it. The word boundary \b matches the edge between a word character and a non-word character, useful for whole-word matches.

With the constructor, remember each backslash must itself be escaped in the string.

Parentheses group part of a pattern so quantifiers and alternation (|) apply to the whole group, and they capture the matched text for later use. RegExp.prototype.test(str) returns a boolean — ideal for validation. String.prototype.match returns the first match (or all matches with the g flag), while matchAll returns an iterator of every match WITH capture groups. replace swaps matched text, supporting $1 backreferences or a replacer function; with a global regex it replaces every occurrence. question: Which statement best describes Groups and capturing?
options: A lookahead asserts what follows without consuming it. Positive lookahead (?=...) matches a position only if the pattern ahead matches; negative lookahead (?!...) matches only if it does NOT. A common use is password rules: assert at least one digit somewhere ahead without removing it from the match. (JavaScript also supports lookbehind (?<=...) / (?<!...) in modern engines.)
